items.title: The Four-Day Week
items.text:
When a software company in Da Nang announced that its staff would work four days a week for the same salary, many people assumed productivity would fall. Six months later, the results suggest the opposite.
According to the company's figures, the amount of work completed per week has stayed roughly the same, while sick days have dropped by almost a third. Staff report that they are less tired and spend fewer hours in unnecessary meetings. "When you know you only have four days, you stop wasting time," says project manager Thu Trang. "We cancelled half our regular meetings and nobody missed them."
Not everyone is convinced, however. Some customers have complained that it is harder to reach the company on Fridays, and the firm has had to introduce a rota so that a small team is always available. A few employees also admit that the longer working days can be exhausting, particularly for parents who have to collect children from school.
Economists point out that the model may suit office-based businesses better than hospitals, shops or factories, where work cannot simply be done faster. Even so, the experiment has sparked a lively debate. Several other firms in the city are now running their own trials, and the company's director says she has no intention of going back. "People are not machines," she argues. "If they come back on Monday rested, they do better work. It's that simple."

qs.q: What happened to the number of sick days?
qs.a: It fell by nearly a third
w: It rose slightly
It stayed the same
qs.why: “sick days have dropped by almost a third.”

qs.q: Why did the company introduce a rota?
qs.a: So customers could still contact them on Fridays
w: So parents could leave early
So staff could attend more meetings
qs.why: “harder to reach the company on Fridays… a small team is always available.”

qs.q: What do economists suggest?
qs.a: The model may not work in every kind of business
w: Factories would benefit most
The model should be made law
qs.why: “the model may suit office-based businesses better than hospitals, shops or factories.”

items.title: Why We Forget Names
items.tvi: Vì sao ta hay quên tên
items.text:
Most of us have experienced it: you are introduced to someone, you shake hands, and ten seconds later their name has completely disappeared. It is embarrassing, but psychologists say it is also entirely normal.
The main reason, they explain, is attention. When we meet someone new, our brains are busy with many other things at once: what the person looks like, what we are going to say, whether we are making a good impression. The name is mentioned only once, often quickly, and it simply never gets stored properly. In other words, we don't forget names; we never learn them in the first place.
Names are also unusually difficult to remember because they are arbitrary. If someone tells you they are a baker, the word connects to lots of things you already know: bread, early mornings, the smell of an oven. A name like 'Hung' or 'Sarah', on the other hand, gives the brain very little to hold on to.
Fortunately, there are simple techniques that help. Repeating the name immediately — "Nice to meet you, Hung" — gives your brain a second chance to record it. Linking the name to an image or to someone else you know with the same name also makes it more memorable. Finally, using the name once more at the end of the conversation can fix it in your memory.
None of these tricks is perfect, but they work far better than the most common strategy, which is hoping for the best.

qs.q: According to psychologists, why do we lose names so quickly?
qs.a: We are not paying full attention when we hear them
w: Our memory gets worse with age
Most names are too long
qs.why: “The main reason, they explain, is attention… it simply never gets stored properly.”

qs.q: Why is a job easier to remember than a name?
qs.a: It connects to things we already know
w: Jobs are mentioned more often
Jobs are usually shorter words
qs.why: “the word connects to lots of things you already know… A name… gives the brain very little to hold on to.”

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude to 'hoping for the best'?
qs.a: It is less effective than the techniques described
w: It is the most reliable strategy
It works for most people
qs.why: “they work far better than the most common strategy, which is hoping for the best.”

items.title: Gap Year: Waste of Time or Life Lesson?
items.tvi: Năm nghỉ trước đại học: phí thời gian hay bài học?
items.text:
After finishing school, Minh Anh surprised her parents by announcing that she would not start university immediately. Instead, she wanted to spend a year working and travelling. Her father was horrified. "He was sure I would never go back to studying," she remembers.
She spent the first six months working in a hotel in Hoi An, saving most of her salary. The job was hard: long shifts, difficult guests, and a manager who rarely said thank you. But she learned to deal with complaints calmly and discovered she was good at solving problems under pressure.
With her savings, she then travelled through Laos and Cambodia, volunteering at a school for two months. Teaching children with almost no resources, she says, taught her more about creativity than any classroom ever had.
Critics of gap years argue that they are a luxury for the wealthy and that students lose their study habits. There is some truth in this: a gap year that consists mainly of parties on a beach is unlikely to be valuable. Universities, however, report that students who take a well-planned year out tend to be more motivated and are less likely to drop out.
Minh Anh is now in her second year of a business degree. Her grades are among the best in her class, and her father has changed his mind. "He tells everyone it was his idea," she laughs.

qs.q: What did Minh Anh learn from her hotel job?
qs.a: How to handle problems when under pressure
w: How to manage a hotel
How to save money while travelling
qs.why: “she learned to deal with complaints calmly and discovered she was good at solving problems under pressure.”

qs.q: What does the writer accept about critics' views?
qs.a: A gap year without a plan may have little value
w: Gap years always cause students to drop out
Only rich students should take a gap year
qs.why: “a gap year that consists mainly of parties on a beach is unlikely to be valuable.”

qs.q: What does the last paragraph tell us about her father?
qs.a: He now feels positive about her decision
w: He still disagrees with her choice
He paid for her travels
qs.why: “her father has changed his mind. He tells everyone it was his idea.”

items.title: The Return of Board Games
items.tvi: Trò chơi bàn cờ trở lại
items.text:
In an age of smartphones and online games, you might expect board games to be disappearing. In fact, the opposite is happening. Sales have grown steadily for over a decade, and board game cafés, where customers pay a small fee to play from a library of hundreds of games, have opened in cities from Seoul to Ho Chi Minh City.
So what explains their popularity? Part of the answer lies in a desire for real-life contact. Many young people spend their working days in front of screens, and sitting around a table with friends offers a welcome break. Unlike online games, board games require players to look at each other, negotiate and laugh together.
The games themselves have also changed. Modern designers have moved away from simple luck-based games towards ones that reward planning and cooperation. In some popular titles, players work together against the game rather than against each other, which makes them attractive to people who dislike competition.
The internet has, ironically, helped too. Online videos explaining the rules make it easy to learn complicated games, and crowdfunding websites allow small designers to raise money without the support of a big company.
Café owner Quang believes the trend will last. "People don't come here just to play," he says. "They come to spend time with people they care about. That never goes out of fashion."

qs.q: What is surprising about board games today, according to the writer?
qs.a: They are becoming more popular despite technology
w: They are mainly played online
They are cheaper than ever before
qs.why: “you might expect board games to be disappearing. In fact, the opposite is happening.”

qs.q: Why might people who dislike competition enjoy modern games?
qs.a: Some games are played as a team against the game
w: The games depend mostly on luck
The games are very short
qs.why: “players work together against the game rather than against each other.”

qs.q: Why does the writer describe the internet's role as ironic?
qs.a: Technology is helping a non-digital hobby
w: Online games have become less popular
The internet makes rules more complicated
qs.why: “The internet has, ironically, helped too.” (công nghệ giúp trò chơi không dùng màn hình)

items.title: Letter to the Editor: Our Disappearing Trees
items.tvi: Thư gửi toà soạn: cây xanh đang biến mất
items.text:
Dear Editor,
I am writing to express my concern about the number of old trees being cut down in our city centre. In the last year alone, at least forty mature trees have been removed from Tran Phu Street to make room for wider pavements and new shops.
The council claims that the trees were unsafe and that new ones will be planted. While I understand that some old trees can be dangerous in storms, I find it hard to believe that every single one was a risk. Moreover, a young tree takes twenty or thirty years to provide the same shade as the ones we have lost.
The consequences are already obvious. Walking along Tran Phu Street at midday in summer is now extremely unpleasant, and several shopkeepers have told me that fewer customers stop there. Studies from other cities show that streets with trees can be several degrees cooler than those without.
I would like to suggest that the council publish an independent report before removing any more trees, and that residents be consulted. I would also urge readers who share my concern to attend the public meeting at the town hall on 12 May.
Yours faithfully,
Nguyen Van Binh

qs.q: What is the council's explanation for cutting the trees?
qs.a: The trees were dangerous
w: The trees were too expensive to maintain
Shopkeepers asked for it
qs.why: “The council claims that the trees were unsafe.”

qs.q: Why is the writer not satisfied with planting new trees?
qs.a: New trees take decades to give the same shade
w: New trees are often unsafe
There is no space for new trees
qs.why: “a young tree takes twenty or thirty years to provide the same shade.”

qs.q: What does the writer want the council to do?
qs.a: Get an independent report and ask residents' opinions
w: Stop building new shops
Plant trees in other cities
qs.why: “publish an independent report… and that residents be consulted.”

items.title: Sleep and Teenagers
items.tvi: Giấc ngủ và tuổi mới lớn
items.text:
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up late and then refuse to get out of bed in the morning. It is tempting to blame laziness or phones, but scientists say biology plays a major part.
During adolescence, the body releases melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, about two hours later than it does in children or adults. As a result, many teenagers genuinely cannot fall asleep before eleven or midnight. Since they still need eight to ten hours of sleep, waking up at six for school leaves them seriously short of rest.
The effects of this are not trivial. Research links lack of sleep in young people to poorer concentration, lower exam results, and even a higher risk of road accidents among new drivers. Some studies also suggest a connection with anxiety and depression.
In response, a number of schools in the United States and Europe have experimented with later start times. One district that moved its school day from 7.30 to 8.30 reported better attendance and a noticeable rise in grades. Not all schools find it easy, though: later starts can cause problems with bus timetables and with parents' working hours.
Phones are not completely innocent, of course. The blue light from screens can delay sleep even further. Experts recommend switching devices off an hour before bed — advice that, admittedly, many adults also ignore.

qs.q: According to scientists, why do teenagers go to bed late?
qs.a: Their bodies produce the sleep hormone later
w: They have too much homework
They are naturally lazy
qs.why: “the body releases melatonin… about two hours later.”

qs.q: What happened in the district that started school later?
qs.a: Attendance and grades improved
w: Students went to bed even later
Parents refused the change
qs.why: “reported better attendance and a noticeable rise in grades.”

qs.q: What does the writer suggest in the last sentence?
qs.a: Adults also don't follow the advice about screens
w: Adults need more sleep than teenagers
Phones are not a real problem
qs.why: “advice that, admittedly, many adults also ignore.”

items.title: The Village That Saved Its School
items.text:
Three years ago, the primary school in the mountain village of Ta Van was about to close. Young families had been moving to the city for work, and the number of pupils had fallen from eighty to just nineteen. The education department argued that it made more sense to send the remaining children by bus to a larger school forty minutes away.
Local people were determined to prevent this. "If the school closes, the village dies," said Mr Sung, whose grandchildren studied there. Residents formed a committee and came up with an unusual plan: they would turn the school into a centre that also served visitors.
With help from a charity, they converted an empty classroom into a small guesthouse. Tourists who stay there pay a fee that goes towards teachers' salaries, and in the afternoons the children practise their English by showing guests around the village. Parents, meanwhile, run cooking and weaving classes for visitors.
The results have exceeded expectations. Pupil numbers have risen to thirty-five, partly because two families moved back after finding work in tourism. The children's English has improved dramatically, and the school has won a regional award for innovation.
There are challenges. Some residents worry that too many tourists could change village life, and the committee now limits the number of guests to six per night. But for now, the school bell still rings every morning — something that seemed impossible three years ago.

qs.q: Why did the education department want to close the school?
qs.a: There were very few pupils left
w: The building was unsafe
There were no teachers
qs.why: “the number of pupils had fallen from eighty to just nineteen.”

qs.q: How does the guesthouse help the school?
qs.a: Guests' fees help pay teachers
w: Teachers live in the guesthouse
It provides classrooms for more pupils
qs.why: “Tourists who stay there pay a fee that goes towards teachers' salaries.”

qs.q: Why does the committee limit the number of guests?
qs.a: To protect traditional village life
w: The guesthouse has only one room
The children cannot speak enough English
qs.why: “Some residents worry that too many tourists could change village life.”

items.title: Do We Really Need to Own a Car?
items.tvi: Ta có thật cần sở hữu ô tô?
items.text:
For previous generations, buying a car was a symbol of success. Today, a growing number of young city dwellers are deciding that it is simply not worth it.
The arguments are largely financial. Once you add up insurance, fuel, parking, repairs and the loss of value over time, owning a car in a big city can cost far more than people realise. A recent survey found that the average urban car is parked for about 95 percent of its life. Meanwhile, ride-hailing apps, car-sharing schemes and improved public transport mean that it is easier than ever to get around without one.
Environmental concerns also play a role, though perhaps a smaller one than is often claimed. When asked why they had not bought a car, only a quarter of respondents mentioned pollution, compared with more than half who mentioned cost.
Car manufacturers are paying attention. Several now offer monthly subscriptions, allowing customers to use a vehicle without buying it and to change models whenever they like. Others are investing in car-sharing businesses themselves.
Of course, the picture looks very different outside the cities. In rural areas, where buses are rare and distances long, a car or motorbike remains a necessity rather than a choice. The trend away from ownership, therefore, may say more about how cities are changing than about a change in people's values.

qs.q: What was the main reason people gave for not buying a car?
qs.a: The cost
w: Pollution
Lack of parking
qs.why: “only a quarter… mentioned pollution, compared with more than half who mentioned cost.”

qs.q: How are some car companies responding?
qs.a: By offering cars on monthly subscriptions
w: By lowering the price of new cars
By building more car parks
qs.why: “Several now offer monthly subscriptions.”

qs.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
qs.a: The trend reflects changes in cities more than in values
w: Everyone will stop owning cars soon
People in the countryside care more about cars
qs.why: “may say more about how cities are changing than about a change in people's values.”

items.title: Learning from Failure
items.text:
When engineer Pham Duc Long's first business went bankrupt in 2015, he felt ashamed. He had borrowed money from relatives, hired twelve people and promised investors rapid growth. Within two years, everything had gone. "I didn't leave the house for weeks," he admits. "I thought everyone was talking about me."
It was a conversation with an older businesswoman that changed his perspective. She told him that she had failed three times before her current company succeeded, and that each failure had taught her something she could never have learned from a book. She encouraged him to write down exactly what had gone wrong.
The list was painful but useful. Long realised that he had spent too much money on an expensive office before he had enough customers, and that he had ignored early warnings from his accountant because he did not want to hear bad news. Above all, he had never properly tested whether people actually wanted his product.
His second company, launched in 2018, started from his kitchen. He spent six months talking to potential customers before building anything. Today it employs sixty people and is profitable.
Long now gives talks at universities about failure. Students, he says, are often surprised that he talks more about his first company than his second. "Success teaches you very little," he tells them. "Failure, if you are honest about it, teaches you everything."

qs.q: How did Long feel immediately after his first business failed?
qs.a: Embarrassed and unwilling to go out
w: Relieved and full of new ideas
Angry with his investors
qs.why: “he felt ashamed… I didn't leave the house for weeks.”

qs.q: Which mistake did Long identify?
qs.a: He didn't check if customers wanted the product
w: He hired too few employees
He listened too much to his accountant
qs.why: “he had never properly tested whether people actually wanted his product.”

qs.q: Why are students surprised by Long's talks?
qs.a: He focuses on his failed company
w: He says success is easy
He criticises universities
qs.why: “he talks more about his first company than his second.”

items.title: Street Food Goes Upmarket
items.tvi: Món ăn đường phố lên đời
items.text:
Not long ago, the idea of paying restaurant prices for a bowl of street food would have seemed ridiculous to most Vietnamese diners. Now, in several major cities, chefs are taking dishes traditionally sold from plastic stools on the pavement and serving them in elegant dining rooms at five times the price.
Supporters say this is a way of showing respect for traditional cooking. Chef Mai Linh, whose restaurant serves a refined version of banh xeo, argues that street food has always been undervalued. "These recipes are as complex as anything in French cuisine," she says. "Why shouldn't they be presented with the same care?" She also points out that she buys ingredients from small local farmers and pays her staff well above the average wage.
Critics are less enthusiastic. Food writer Tran Hai believes that something important is lost when street food moves indoors. "Part of the experience is the noise, the crowd, the woman who has cooked the same dish for forty years," he says. "Put it on a white plate and it becomes something else." Others worry that rising prices could eventually push ordinary vendors out of business.
The debate is unlikely to be settled soon. What is clear is that the two worlds can exist side by side. On the street outside Mai Linh's restaurant, a vendor still sells banh xeo for a fraction of the price — and on most evenings, her queue is just as long.

qs.q: Why does Chef Mai Linh think street food deserves careful presentation?
qs.a: Its recipes are just as complex as other cuisines
w: It is cheaper to produce
Tourists prefer formal restaurants
qs.why: “These recipes are as complex as anything in French cuisine.”

qs.q: What is Tran Hai's main concern?
qs.a: The atmosphere of eating on the street is lost
w: The food in restaurants is less fresh
Restaurant chefs are poorly paid
qs.why: “Part of the experience is the noise, the crowd… Put it on a white plate and it becomes something else.”

qs.q: What does the last paragraph suggest?
qs.a: Street vendors and upmarket restaurants can both succeed
w: Street vendors are losing customers
The restaurant will soon close
qs.why: “the two worlds can exist side by side… her queue is just as long.”

items.title: The Return of the Night Train
items.text:
For most of the past thirty years, the overnight train in Europe seemed to be heading for extinction. Cheap flights could take passengers across the continent in a couple of hours, and rail companies cut sleeper services one after another, arguing that they were too expensive to run. Yet recently, something unexpected has happened: night trains are coming back.
The reasons are partly environmental. A growing number of travellers, particularly younger ones, feel uncomfortable about the carbon emissions of short flights, and a train journey produces only a fraction of them. But the appeal is not purely about the climate. Many passengers simply enjoy the experience. You board in the evening, have dinner, sleep in a proper bed and wake up in another country, without the queues and security checks of an airport. Business travellers point out that they arrive in the city centre ready for a morning meeting, having lost no working time.
That is the romantic version. The reality can be less comfortable. Some of the newly launched services use old carriages, and passengers have complained about broken air conditioning, thin walls and delays of several hours. Prices are another issue. A private compartment can cost considerably more than a flight, which means that, for families on a budget, the night train often remains a luxury rather than a realistic alternative.
Rail operators insist that these are early difficulties. New carriages are being built, and several governments have begun to offer financial support, recognising that sleeper trains could help them meet climate targets. Some experts, however, remain sceptical. They argue that without changes to the way flights are taxed, trains will never be able to compete on price, and that night services will stay a niche product for a relatively wealthy minority.
What is clear is that the night train has moved from being a symbol of the past to a test of the future. Whether it becomes an ordinary way to travel will depend less on nostalgia than on investment, reliability and the price of a ticket.

qs.q: Why did many night train services close in the past?
qs.a: They cost too much to operate compared with cheap flights
w: Passengers complained about the old carriages
Governments wanted to reduce train travel
There were too many security problems
qs.why: Đoạn 1: “Cheap flights… rail companies cut sleeper services… too expensive to run.”

qs.q: According to the article, business travellers like night trains because
qs.a: they can arrive ready to work without losing working hours
w: their companies pay for private compartments
they can hold meetings on the train
trains are faster than flights
qs.why: “arrive in the city centre ready for a morning meeting, having lost no working time.”

qs.q: What does the writer mean by “That is the romantic version”?
qs.a: The description so far has ignored the problems
w: Night trains are popular with couples
The writer prefers trains to planes
Most passengers travel for holidays
qs.why: Câu chuyển ý sang đoạn kể các bất tiện: điều hòa hỏng, tường mỏng, trễ giờ.

qs.q: Why is the night train still “a luxury” for some families?
qs.a: Private compartments can be more expensive than flying
w: Children are not allowed in sleeper carriages
The trains do not run during school holidays
Tickets must be booked months ahead
qs.why: “A private compartment can cost considerably more than a flight.”

qs.q: The word “sceptical” in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
qs.a: doubtful
w: enthusiastic
well informed
angry
qs.why: sceptical = hoài nghi, không tin hẳn = doubtful.

qs.q: What does the writer conclude about the future of night trains?
qs.a: It depends mainly on practical factors such as cost and reliability
w: They will certainly replace short flights
They will disappear again within a few years
Their success depends on people's love of the past
qs.why: “will depend less on nostalgia than on investment, reliability and the price of a ticket.”

items.title: Learning to Fail
items.text:
When Linh Pham started teaching chemistry at a secondary school in Hanoi, she noticed something that worried her. Her brightest students were often the most afraid of getting an answer wrong. If a problem looked unfamiliar, they would rather leave the page blank than risk a mistake. "They had learned that being clever means being right the first time," she says. "So anything difficult felt like a threat."
She decided to try an experiment. Once a week, she gave her class a problem that was deliberately too hard for them, and she graded not the answer but the attempt: how many different approaches students tried, how clearly they explained what had gone wrong, and what they would do differently next time. At first, the students hated it. Several parents complained that their children's grades were being damaged by "impossible" questions.
By the end of the term, however, the atmosphere in the classroom had changed. Students began to talk openly about their mistakes, and some even started to enjoy the weekly challenge. Linh noticed that their results on ordinary tests had improved too, especially on questions that required them to apply knowledge in new situations.
Psychologists have a name for what Linh was encouraging: productive struggle. Research suggests that when learners wrestle with a problem before being shown the solution, they often understand it more deeply than if they had been taught the method first. The key, experts say, is that the struggle must be manageable. A task that is slightly beyond a student's ability can build confidence; one that is completely out of reach is more likely to destroy it.
Linh admits that the approach is not suitable for every lesson, and that some students still find it stressful. But she has no plans to give it up. "In real life, nobody gives you the answer at the back of the book," she says. "I want my students to be comfortable not knowing, at least for a while."

qs.q: What did Linh notice about her brightest students at first?
qs.a: They avoided problems they might get wrong
w: They finished their work too quickly
They did not respect their teacher
They were bored by easy questions
qs.why: “they would rather leave the page blank than risk a mistake.”

qs.q: In Linh's weekly experiment, students were graded on
qs.a: their approach and their reflection on mistakes
w: whether the final answer was correct
how fast they finished
how well they worked in groups
qs.why: “graded not the answer but the attempt: how many different approaches… what had gone wrong…”

qs.q: How did some parents react at first?
qs.a: They thought the hard questions were unfair to their children
w: They asked for more difficult homework
They wanted to observe the lessons
They supported the experiment immediately
qs.why: “Several parents complained that their children's grades were being damaged by ‘impossible’ questions.”

qs.q: What improvement did Linh see in ordinary tests?
qs.a: Students were better at using knowledge in unfamiliar situations
w: Students made no mistakes at all
Students remembered more facts
Students finished tests more quickly
qs.why: “especially on questions that required them to apply knowledge in new situations.”

qs.q: According to experts, what makes struggle “productive”?
qs.a: The task is difficult but still within reach
w: The teacher gives the method first
Students work alone without help
The problems are completely new every time
qs.why: “the struggle must be manageable… slightly beyond a student's ability can build confidence.”

qs.q: What does Linh's final comment suggest about her aim?
qs.a: She wants students to cope with uncertainty
w: She wants students to stop using textbooks
She thinks answers should never be given
She plans to make all lessons harder
qs.why: “I want my students to be comfortable not knowing, at least for a while.”

items.title: Are Cities Too Noisy?
items.text:
Ask people what they dislike about living in a big city and most will mention traffic, pollution or the cost of housing. Fewer will mention noise, yet according to the World Health Organization, it is one of the most serious environmental threats to health in many urban areas.
The problem is not only that noise is annoying. Long-term exposure to loud traffic, construction and nightlife has been linked to poor sleep, raised blood pressure and an increased risk of heart disease. Children who attend schools near busy roads or airports have been found, in some studies, to learn to read more slowly than children in quieter areas. Because these effects build up gradually, people often fail to connect them with the sounds around them.
Part of the difficulty is that cities are designed to be lively. Restaurants, bars and street markets bring life and money to neighbourhoods, and few residents would want to live somewhere completely silent. The question is therefore not how to remove noise altogether but how to manage it.
Some cities have taken creative steps. Paris has tested "noise radars" that identify vehicles exceeding sound limits, in the same way that speed cameras catch fast drivers. Other cities have introduced quiet road surfaces, planted trees along major roads and limited delivery hours in residential streets. Building regulations can also help: thicker windows and careful planning of where bedrooms face can reduce the noise people experience at home.
Critics argue that such measures mainly benefit wealthier districts, while poorer neighbourhoods, which are often closer to motorways and industrial zones, continue to suffer. Campaigners say that noise should be treated as a question of fairness as well as health, and that the people most exposed to it are often the least able to move away.
Noise may never generate the same headlines as air pollution. But for millions of city dwellers who lie awake listening to engines and car horns, it is far from a minor issue.

qs.q: What point does the writer make in the first paragraph?
qs.a: Noise is a serious problem that people often overlook
w: Most people move to cities for the noise
Noise is the main reason people leave cities
Traffic is less harmful than noise
qs.why: “Fewer will mention noise, yet… it is one of the most serious environmental threats.”

qs.q: Why do people often fail to link health problems with noise?
qs.a: The effects develop slowly over time
w: Doctors rarely ask about noise
The effects only appear in children
People get used to noise in a few days
qs.why: “Because these effects build up gradually, people often fail to connect them.”

qs.q: According to the writer, the aim of city noise policy should be to
qs.a: control noise rather than eliminate it
w: close bars and markets at night
make cities completely silent
move schools away from city centres
qs.why: “The question is therefore not how to remove noise altogether but how to manage it.”

qs.q: How do Paris's “noise radars” work?
qs.a: They detect vehicles that are too loud
w: They measure noise inside homes
They warn residents before construction starts
They reduce the sound of traffic
qs.why: “identify vehicles exceeding sound limits, in the same way that speed cameras catch fast drivers.”

qs.q: What criticism of anti-noise measures is mentioned?
qs.a: They help richer areas more than poorer ones
w: They are too expensive for any city
They make cities less lively
They are not based on research
qs.why: “such measures mainly benefit wealthier districts, while poorer neighbourhoods… continue to suffer.”

qs.q: What is the purpose of the final paragraph?
qs.a: To stress that noise is an important problem despite little attention
w: To suggest that air pollution is less serious
To describe the writer's own sleeping problems
To predict that noise will soon disappear
qs.why: “it is far from a minor issue” cho hàng triệu người.

items.title: The Shop with No Packaging
items.text:
When Mai and her sister opened a grocery shop in Ho Chi Minh City selling everything without plastic packaging, friends told them it would close within a year. Customers, they said, were too busy to bring their own jars and bags. Four years later, the shop is still open, and the sisters are planning a second branch.
The idea is simple. Rice, beans, nuts, cooking oil, shampoo and washing-up liquid are stored in large containers, and customers fill their own bottles or bags, paying by weight. Those who forget their containers can borrow glass jars, which they return on their next visit. "At the beginning we lost about a third of the jars," Mai admits. "Now almost all of them come back. People like being trusted."
The sisters say that the hardest part was not the customers but the suppliers. Many producers were used to delivering goods in small plastic packets and were unwilling to change. Mai spent months visiting farms and small factories, persuading them to deliver in large sacks or reusable drums. Some refused; others agreed only after the shop promised to buy larger quantities.
Prices in the shop are not always lower than in supermarkets. Some products are cheaper because customers do not pay for packaging, but others, especially organic goods, cost more. The sisters are honest about this. "We are not trying to compete with big chains on price," Mai says. "We are offering a different way of shopping for people who care about waste."
Sceptics point out that a single shop makes little difference to the enormous amount of plastic produced in the country. Mai does not disagree, but she believes that small businesses can influence larger ones. Last year, a supermarket nearby started selling rice from refill stations, and she likes to think her shop played a part. "We will never change the world on our own," she says, "but we can show that another way is possible."

qs.q: What did the sisters' friends predict?
qs.a: Customers would not bother to bring containers
w: The shop would be too expensive
Suppliers would refuse to work with them
The shop would need a second branch quickly
qs.why: “Customers, they said, were too busy to bring their own jars and bags.”

qs.q: What does Mai's comment about the jars suggest?
qs.a: Customers became more responsible when they were trusted
w: The shop stopped lending jars
Glass jars were too expensive to replace
Most customers kept the jars as souvenirs
qs.why: Lúc đầu mất 1/3 lọ, giờ gần như trả hết: “People like being trusted.”

qs.q: Why was dealing with suppliers difficult?
qs.a: Many were reluctant to change how they delivered goods
w: They charged too much for large sacks
They were located too far from the city
They did not trust the sisters to pay
qs.why: “Many producers were used to delivering goods in small plastic packets and were unwilling to change.”

qs.q: What is true about prices in the shop?
qs.a: Some items are cheaper and some are more expensive than in supermarkets
w: Everything is cheaper than in supermarkets
Prices are the same as in big chains
Only organic goods are cheaper
qs.why: “Some products are cheaper… but others, especially organic goods, cost more.”

qs.q: How does Mai respond to the sceptics' view?
qs.a: She accepts it but thinks small shops can influence bigger businesses
w: She says her shop has already solved the problem
She thinks supermarkets should be closed
She refuses to discuss the issue
qs.why: “Mai does not disagree, but she believes that small businesses can influence larger ones.”

qs.q: The phrase “played a part” in the last paragraph means
qs.a: had some influence
w: acted in a play
lost some money
made a decision
qs.why: play a part = góp phần, có ảnh hưởng.

items.title: Working from Home: Two Years Later
items.tvi: Làm việc tại nhà: hai năm sau
items.text:
When the software company where I work allowed everyone to work from home permanently, I was delighted. No more ninety-minute commutes, no more noisy open-plan office, no more queues for the lift. Two years later, my feelings are more mixed.
The benefits are real. I have gained roughly fifteen hours a week that I used to spend in traffic, and I use some of that time to exercise and cook proper meals. I can concentrate for long periods without interruptions, and I am, by any measurable standard, more productive than I was in the office. My manager agrees.
What I underestimated was how much I would miss the small, unplanned conversations. In the office, I would bump into colleagues in the kitchen and end up solving a problem that had nothing to do with my own work. Those moments rarely happen on video calls, which are always scheduled and usually have an agenda. Newer colleagues seem to suffer most. A junior developer who joined last year told me she had never met half of her team in person and felt she was learning much more slowly than she would have in an office.
There is also the problem of boundaries. When your kitchen table is your desk, it is surprisingly easy to answer one more email at ten o'clock at night. I have had to set strict rules for myself: I close the laptop at six and I do not check messages on my phone at weekends.
My company has now introduced two "office days" a week, and I was surprised to find that I look forward to them. The arrangement seems to offer the best of both worlds: quiet days for focused work and busy days for meetings, training and the kind of chance conversations that keep a team connected. Working from home, I have learned, is not simply better or worse than the office. It depends on what kind of work you are trying to do.

qs.q: How did the writer feel when home working became permanent?
qs.a: Very pleased
w: Worried about the change
Indifferent
Disappointed
qs.why: “I was delighted.”

qs.q: What does the writer say about their productivity at home?
qs.a: It has increased
w: It has fallen because of distractions
It is impossible to measure
It is the same as before
qs.why: “I am, by any measurable standard, more productive than I was in the office.”

qs.q: What does the writer miss most about the office?
qs.a: Informal conversations that happened by chance
w: The open-plan layout
Scheduled meetings with an agenda
The journey to work
qs.why: “how much I would miss the small, unplanned conversations.”

qs.q: Why does the writer mention the junior developer?
qs.a: To show that new employees may find remote work harder
w: To complain about her performance
To explain why video calls are useful
To show that young people prefer working from home
qs.why: “Newer colleagues seem to suffer most… learning much more slowly.”

qs.q: What problem does “boundaries” refer to?
qs.a: Separating work time from personal time
w: Arguments with family members
Finding space for a desk at home
Limits set by the company on overtime
qs.why: Bàn ăn thành bàn làm việc nên dễ trả lời email lúc 10 giờ tối.

qs.q: What is the writer's final view?
qs.a: Whether home or office is better depends on the type of work
w: Everyone should return to the office full time
Working from home is always more productive
Office days are a waste of time
qs.why: “It depends on what kind of work you are trying to do.”
